questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with painful grouped vesicles on an erythematous base on her labia majora, associated with inguinal lymphadenopathy and fever. She reports a similar episode 6 months ago. The most appropriate first-line treatment is:
opts: Acyclovir 400 mg three times daily for 5 days
Valacyclovir 1 g twice daily for 7 days
Famciclovir 500 mg twice daily for 7 days
questions.exp: Recurrent genital herpes (HSV-2) is treated with episodic antiviral therapy. Acyclovir 400 mg TID × 5 days is the WHO/CDC first-line regimen for recurrent episodes. Valacyclovir 500 mg BD × 3 days is also acceptable but not listed here. Penciclovir cream is for orolabial herpes only.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male presents with a painless ulcer on the glans penis with indurated margins and bilateral non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. Dark-field microscopy reveals corkscrew-shaped organisms. The drug of choice is:
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose
questions.exp: Primary syphilis (Treponema pallidum) is treated with Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM as a single dose. This is the recommended CDC/IADVL regimen. Doxycycline is used in penicillin-allergic patients. Azithromycin has emerging resistance and is not recommended first-line.

questions.q: A 32-year-old man from Tamil Nadu presents with a painless plaque on the cheek with loss of sensation, thickened great auricular nerve, and slit-skin smear showing solid-staining bacilli with a bacterial index of 4+. He is classified as:
questions.exp: A BI of 4+ confirms multibacillary (MB) leprosy regardless of lesion count. WHO MDT for MB leprosy consists of Rifampicin 600 mg monthly + Clofazimine 300 mg monthly + Dapsone 100 mg daily + Clofazimine 50 mg daily for 12 months. A BI ≥ 2 classifies as MB leprosy.

questions.q: A leprosy patient on clofazimine therapy develops erythematous tender nodules over the face, forearms, and thighs with fever, malaise, and raised ESR. The most likely diagnosis and management is:
questions.exp: Erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL, Type 2 reaction) presents with crops of tender erythematous nodules, systemic symptoms, and raised ESR in MB leprosy patients. Thalidomide 100–400 mg/day is the most effective treatment for ENL and is recommended for males. Prednisolone is used when thalidomide is contraindicated.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with recurrent flaccid blisters over the trunk and oral erosions. Biopsy shows suprabasal acantholysis, and direct immunofluorescence reveals intercellular IgG deposits in a 'fishnet' pattern. The autoantibody most likely responsible is directed against:
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris predominantly involves desmoglein 3 (oral mucosa involvement). Anti-desmoglein 3 antibodies cause loss of keratinocyte adhesion in the suprabasal layer. Anti-BP180 is seen in bullous pemphigoid; anti-laminin 332 in mucous membrane pemphigoid; anti-type VII collagen in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita.

questions.q: A 70-year-old diabetic woman presents with tense bullae on an urticarial base on the lower abdomen and thighs. Biopsy shows subepidermal blister with eosinophils, and direct IF shows linear IgG and C3 at the basement membrane zone. The best initial systemic treatment is:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) presents with tense bullae, eosinophilia, subepidermal split, and linear IgG/C3 at BMZ (anti-BP180/BP230). First-line treatment is systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone 0.5–1 mg/kg/day). Dapsone and tetracycline+niacinamide are alternatives for mild-moderate disease. Azathioprine is a steroid-sparing agent.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with intensely pruritic vesicles on extensor surfaces of elbows, knees, and buttocks. She also has symptoms of malabsorption. Biopsy of perilesional skin shows granular IgA deposits at the dermal papillae. The most effective treatment is:
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is associated with coeliac disease and shows granular IgA at dermal papillary tips on DIF. Treatment is dapsone for rapid symptom control and strict gluten-free diet for long-term management and prevention of intestinal lymphoma. Dapsone does not treat the underlying enteropathy.

questions.q: A 60-year-old farmer presents with an irregularly shaped pearly nodule with telangiectasia and a rolled border on the nose. He has a long history of sun exposure. Dermoscopy reveals arborizing vessels and maple leaf-like structures. The diagnosis and preferred treatment is:
opts: Basal cell carcinoma – Mohs micrographic surgery
Squamous cell carcinoma – wide local excision
questions.exp: Nodular basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common skin cancer, typically on sun-exposed areas in elderly patients. Mohs micrographic surgery provides the highest cure rate (99%) and tissue conservation, especially for high-risk areas like the nose (H zone). Dermoscopy shows arborizing vessels, blue-grey ovoid nests, and maple leaf areas.

questions.q: A 65-year-old immunosuppressed renal transplant recipient presents with rapidly growing indurated ulcerated lesion on the dorsum of the hand with perineural invasion on histology. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is positive. This lesion is classified as high-risk SCC because of:
opts: Location on hand, diameter >2 cm, immunosuppression, and perineural invasion
questions.exp: High-risk SCC features include: diameter >2 cm, depth >6 mm, poor differentiation, perineural/lymphovascular invasion, recurrent lesion, immunosuppression, and location on ear, lip, or non-sun-exposed sites. Organ transplant recipients have 65–250x higher risk of SCC. Wide excision with 6–10 mm margins and lymph node evaluation is required.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with pigmented macule on the sole with the ABCDE criteria: asymmetry, irregular border, variegated color, diameter 8 mm, and recent elevation. Excisional biopsy reveals Breslow thickness of 1.8 mm, Clark level IV, no ulceration. Appropriate management is:
opts: Wide local excision with 2 cm margins + sentinel lymph node biopsy
Wide local excision with 1 cm margins only
questions.exp: For melanoma with Breslow thickness 1.01–2.0 mm (T2), guidelines recommend wide local excision with 1–2 cm margins and sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB). SLNB is recommended for melanomas >1 mm thick. Clark level IV indicates invasion into reticular dermis. CO2 laser and imiquimod are not appropriate for invasive melanoma.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman develops widespread erythema, target lesions, and mucosal erosions over 3 days following starting trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a UTI. She has fever, conjunctival involvement, and skin detachment of 15% BSA. This condition is:
questions.exp: SJS is defined by epidermal detachment of <10% BSA with mucosal involvement (typically 2+ sites). TEN involves >30% BSA. SJS/TEN overlap is 10–30% BSA. The most common triggers are sulfonamides, anticonvulsants, allopurinol, and NSAIDs. Immediate drug withdrawal is critical; management includes supportive care in a burns unit.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus presents with a butterfly-shaped malar rash. ANA is positive at 1:640 with anti-dsDNA antibodies. For her photosensitive rash, the most appropriate sunscreen and hydroxychloroquine dose are:
opts: No sunscreen needed if on hydroxychloroquine
questions.exp: SLE skin disease requires strict photoprotection (broad-spectrum SPF 50+, UVA+UVB protection). Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is the standard antimalarial for cutaneous lupus, dosed at ≤5 mg/kg/day to minimize retinal toxicity. Annual ophthalmologic monitoring is essential. Anti-dsDNA antibodies correlate with lupus nephritis activity.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with skin tightening, Raynaud's phenomenon, telangiectasia, and dysphagia. ANA shows anticentromere pattern. She most likely has:
questions.exp: Limited cutaneous SSc (CREST syndrome: Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia) is associated with anticentromere antibodies (ACA). Diffuse SSc is associated with anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) and has worse prognosis with internal organ involvement. ACA predicts pulmonary arterial hypertension risk.

questions.q: A 10-year-old boy presents with scaling of the scalp with broken-off hairs 2–3 mm from the scalp ('black dot pattern'), kerion formation, and occipital lymphadenopathy. KOH mount shows endothrix pattern. The causative organism is most likely:
questions.exp: Trichophyton tonsurans causes endothrix tinea capitis (black dot ringworm) with spores inside the hair shaft. T. violaceum also causes endothrix. Microsporum canis causes ectothrix (spores on hair surface) and fluoresces green under Wood's lamp. T. schoenleinii causes favus (scutula). Treatment is oral griseofulvin or terbinafine.

questions.q: A 35-year-old HIV-positive man (CD4 = 80 cells/μL) presents with painless white plaques on the tongue that cannot be scraped off, with corrugated/hairy appearance on the lateral borders. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Oral hairy leukoplakia (OHL) caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) presents as corrugated white plaques on the lateral borders of the tongue that cannot be removed, unlike oral candidiasis (thrush) which scrapes off. OHL is a marker of immunosuppression (CD4 <200). It is generally asymptomatic and resolves with antiretroviral therapy.

questions.q: A 6-year-old child presents with honey-colored crusts over eroded vesiculopustular lesions around the nose and mouth. Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in clusters. The drug of choice for localized lesions is:
questions.exp: Non-bullous impetigo (most commonly Staphylococcus aureus, sometimes Streptococcus pyogenes) presents with honey-colored crusts. Topical mupirocin 2% TID for 5 days is first-line for localized disease. Oral antibiotics (flucloxacillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate) are reserved for extensive disease. Topical fusidic acid is an alternative.

questions.q: A 50-year-old diabetic develops a rapidly spreading bright red, warm, non-pitting edema of the lower leg with a sharply demarcated raised border. He has fever and chills. The most likely diagnosis and causative organism are:
questions.exp: Erysipelas is characterized by a sharply demarcated, raised, bright red plaque with clear borders, caused almost exclusively by Group A Streptococcus. Cellulitis has indistinct borders and is usually deeper. The face and lower legs are most commonly affected. Treatment is penicillin (benzylpenicillin IV or amoxicillin orally).

questions.q: A patient with advanced HIV (CD4 = 30) presents with multiple violaceous plaques on the lower extremities and palate. Biopsy shows vascular proliferation with extravasated red blood cells, hemosiderin deposits, and spindle-shaped cells. HHV-8 PCR is positive. This is:
questions.exp: AIDS-associated Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is caused by HHV-8 (KSHV). It presents with violaceous/brown-black patches, plaques, and nodules, frequently involving the lower extremities, face, and oral cavity. Histology shows spindle cells, slit-like vascular spaces, and hemosiderin. ART initiation is key; localized disease may be treated with radiotherapy or intralesional chemotherapy.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with well-demarcated, scaly, erythematous plaques on the elbows, knees, and scalp with nail pitting. She is pregnant (28 weeks). The safest systemic treatment option for severe disease is:
questions.exp: Ciclosporin A is the preferred systemic agent for severe psoriasis in pregnancy. Methotrexate is absolutely contraindicated (teratogenic, abortifacient). Acitretin is teratogenic with very long washout period (>2 years). Mycophenolate mofetil is also contraindicated in pregnancy. Ciclosporin has a reasonable safety profile based on transplant data.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man with plaque psoriasis develops joint pain, morning stiffness, and pencil-in-cup deformity of DIP joints on X-ray. He has sausage digits (dactylitis). The most appropriate biologic for both skin and joint disease is:
questions.exp: Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) with pencil-in-cup deformity and dactylitis requires treatment that addresses both skin and joint disease. IL-17A inhibitors (secukinumab, ixekizumab) and TNF inhibitors (adalimumab, etanercept) have approval for both plaque psoriasis and PsA. Dupilumab is for atopic dermatitis; omalizumab for urticaria; mepolizumab for eosinophilic conditions.

questions.q: A 4-year-old child presents with intensely pruritic eczematous lesions on the face, antecubital and popliteal fossae. IgE is markedly elevated. Family history of asthma. The scoring system used to assess severity of this condition is:
questions.exp: Atopic dermatitis severity is measured using SCORAD (SCORing Atopic Dermatitis), which assesses extent (A), intensity (B), and subjective symptoms (C): SCORAD = A/5 + 7B/2 + C. PASI is used for psoriasis. DLQI measures quality of life impact. EASI (Eczema Area and Severity Index) is another validated scoring tool for AD.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with symmetrical hypopigmented patches on the face and dorsum of hands with complete loss of pigmentation (milk-white). Wood's lamp examination shows chalk-white fluorescence. Dermoscopy reveals perifollicular pigment retention. The mechanism of pigment loss is:
opts: Defective melanin synthesis without melanocyte loss
Melanocyte migration failure from neural crest
questions.exp: Vitiligo involves autoimmune CD8+ T-cell-mediated destruction of melanocytes. Antibodies against melanocyte antigens (tyrosinase, MART-1) are also detected. Wood's lamp shows chalk-white enhancement. Perifollicular pigment retention on dermoscopy indicates spared follicular melanocyte reservoirs — a good prognostic sign for repigmentation. Pityriasis alba and tinea versicolor show partial pigment loss.

questions.q: A 32-year-old pregnant woman (third trimester) develops brownish-gray symmetrical hyperpigmentation on the cheeks, upper lip, and forehead that worsens with sun exposure. The best long-term management after delivery is:
opts: Topical azelaic acid 20% alone during pregnancy
questions.exp: Melasma requires strict photoprotection. The Kligman's modified formula (tri-combination: HQ 4% + tretinoin 0.05% + fluocinolone acetonide 0.01%) is the gold-standard first-line depigmenting agent post-delivery. During pregnancy, topical azelaic acid 20% is the safest option. Chemical peels and laser are adjunctive therapies after first-line treatment fails.

questions.q: A 22-year-old man presents with painful genital ulcers with a soft base, non-indurated, undermined edges, and exquisitely tender unilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy (bubo). Gram stain of pus shows 'school of fish' pattern. The causative organism and treatment are:
questions.exp: Chancroid caused by Haemophilus ducreyi presents with painful soft ulcers with undermined edges and tender suppurative inguinal bubo. Gram stain shows gram-negative coccobacilli in 'school of fish' or 'railroad track' pattern. Treatment: azithromycin 1 g single dose, or ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD × 3 days, or ceftriaxone 250 mg IM single dose.

questions.q: A patient presents with chronic painless ulcer on the genitalia with beefy-red granulation tissue, rolled edges, and no lymphadenopathy. Donovan bodies are seen within mononuclear cells on tissue smear. The treatment of choice is:
opts: Azithromycin 1 g weekly for minimum 3 weeks
Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM weekly × 3
questions.exp: Donovanosis (granuloma inguinale) caused by Klebsiella granulomatis presents with painless beefy-red ulcers, no lymphadenopathy, and Donovan bodies (intracytoplasmic gram-negative coccobacilli in macrophages). Azithromycin 1 g weekly (or 500 mg/day) is the CDC recommended regimen until all lesions heal. Doxycycline is an alternative.

questions.q: A 19-year-old woman presents with pruritic flesh-colored papules around the introitus and perianal area with cauliflower morphology. She has multiple sexual partners. PCR identifies HPV types 6 and 11. The safest topical treatment she can self-apply is:
questions.exp: Condylomata acuminata (genital warts) caused by low-risk HPV 6 and 11. Imiquimod 5% cream (TID, 3×/week, up to 16 weeks) is patient-applied and immunomodulatory. Podophyllin must be applied by a clinician and is not for home use. TCA is provider-applied. 5-FU is not FDA-approved for genital warts. Sinecatechins (Polyphenon E) is another patient-applied option.

questions.q: A 48-year-old man presents with cutaneous sarcoidosis showing lupus pernio (violaceous plaques on the nose and cheeks). Serum ACE is elevated. Chest X-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. The most appropriate initial treatment is:
questions.exp: Lupus pernio is a specific cutaneous manifestation of sarcoidosis associated with systemic involvement (pulmonary, bone, eye). Oral corticosteroids are the standard first-line treatment for systemic sarcoidosis. Topical/intralesional steroids are used for limited skin disease only. Antimalarials (hydroxychloroquine) are second-line, and TNF inhibitors (adalimumab) for refractory cases.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man undergoing PUVA therapy for psoriasis develops multiple small pigmented macules on sun-exposed areas. He is at increased risk for:
questions.exp: Long-term PUVA therapy (psoralens + UVA) significantly increases the risk of squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the skin, particularly in the genital area (scrotal SCC). The risk increases with cumulative number of treatments (>200 sessions). Melanoma risk may also be increased. Patients require regular skin surveillance and genital protection during treatment.

questions.q: A patient on isotretinoin for severe nodular acne develops myalgia, elevated CK, and liver enzymes. The dose is 1 mg/kg/day. The most important laboratory monitoring parameter that should prompt dose reduction or cessation is:
questions.exp: Isotretinoin can cause hypertriglyceridemia, which at very high levels (>800 mg/dL) risks acute pancreatitis and is an indication to stop treatment. Liver enzyme elevation (>3× ULN) and severe hypercholesterolemia also warrant consideration of stopping. Monitoring at baseline and 4–8 weekly: lipid panel, LFTs, CBC, blood glucose, and urine pregnancy test (females).

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman with androgenetic alopecia presents with progressive diffuse thinning at the crown with preservation of the frontal hairline. Dermoscopy shows peripilar signs, hair diameter diversity, and yellow dots. The most effective topical treatment is:
opts: Minoxidil 5% solution/foam applied once or twice daily
questions.exp: Female pattern hair loss (FPHL/AGA) is treated with topical minoxidil 2–5% (once or twice daily) as the only FDA-approved topical treatment. Finasteride and dutasteride are not FDA-approved for women and are contraindicated in pregnancy. Spironolactone is used off-label. Minoxidil prolongs anagen phase and increases hair follicle size.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman is referred for patch testing. She develops a reaction at 96 hours at the site of application of an allergen: +2 reaction (erythema, edema, papules). This reaction type is:
questions.exp: Allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) and patch testing reactions represent Type IV (delayed-type/cell-mediated) hypersensitivity. Sensitization occurs on first exposure; elicitation on re-exposure involves CD4+ (and CD8+) T lymphocytes releasing cytokines causing eczematous reaction at 48–96 hours. Type I is immediate (urticaria, anaphylaxis). The ICDRG grading: +1 (erythema, edema), +2 (+papules), +3 (+vesicles).
